title: Frequency arrays
overview: Module 13 teaches the frequency array. It is an array where the index is the value you care about, and the element stores how many times that value appeared, or just whether it appeared. After one pass over the data, you can answer "is x there?" or "how many x?" instantly, with no searching. This trick comes up again and again in later problems.

concepts.explain: `freq[x]` belongs to the number `x`. When you see `x`, you update `freq[x]` directly. No loop is needed to find its place.
The array must start with all zeros. Write `int freq[N] = {0};` inside a function. Global arrays start at zero on their own.
`freq[x] = 1` only marks that `x` was seen. `freq[x]++` counts how many times it was seen. Pick the one the problem needs.
For lowercase letters, `ch - 'a'` maps `a`..`z` to 0..25, so a 26-slot array is enough. Add `'a'` to turn an index back into a letter.
Once the array is built, each question is a single lookup: `freq[x]`.
The array must be bigger than the largest possible value. Values up to 10^5 need about 100001 slots.

files.title: Presence array with yes/no queries
files.what: Marks which numbers are in the array, prints the marks for 0 to 9, then answers queries asking whether a number is present.
steps: For each `a[i]`, set `freq[a[i]] = 1` to mark it as present.
Print `i` and `freq[i]` for `i` from 0 to 9, so you can see the marks.
Read `m` queries. For each `x`, print `YES` if `freq[x] == 1`, otherwise `NO`.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(max value)
files.output_note: The first 10 lines are `value mark`. Only 2, 3, 4 and 7 show `1`, and the repeated 4 is still just `1`. Then come the answers `4 YES`, `5 NO` and `7 YES`.
files.watch_out: A value of 100000 or more would write past the end of `freq`. Always check the limits before choosing the array size.

check.q: Why does 4 show 1 and not 2, even though it appears twice?
check.a: The code sets `freq[x] = 1` instead of adding 1, so it only records presence.

files.title: Frequency Array (count 1..M)
files.what: Counts how many times each number from 1 to M appears. This is the counting version of the frequency array.
steps: `int f[100000];` is global, so every slot starts at 0.
Read each number and do `f[a[i]] += 1` in the same loop.
Print `f[1]`, `f[2]`, and so on up to `f[m]`, one per line.
files.output_note: Line i is the count of i: `2` (two 1s), `1` (one 2), `3` (three 3s), `2` (two 4s).
files.watch_out: The array `a` isn't really needed. You could read into a temporary `x` and do `f[x]++`.

check.q: What would line 5 show if M were 5 with the same numbers?
check.a: `0`, because 5 never appears and global arrays start at zero.

files.title: Distinct letters in a string
files.what: Finds which lowercase letters appear in a fixed string and how many different letters there are. It uses a 26-slot presence array.
steps: The string is hard-coded as `"aaaaaagggggccjcc"`, and `f[26]` starts at zeros.
For each character, `ch - 'a'` gives its slot, and that slot is set to 1.
Loop over the 26 slots. Add each `f[i]` to `cnt`, and if `f[i]` is 1, print the letter `i + 'a'`.
Print `cnt`, the number of different letters.
files.output_note: `a 1`, `c 1`, `g 1` and `j 1` come out in alphabetical order, even though `g` comes before `c` in the string. The last line is `4`.
files.watch_out: Only lowercase letters are safe. An uppercase letter or a digit would give a negative index or one above 25.

check.q: Why do the letters come out sorted?
check.a: The second loop goes through the slots in order from 0 (`a`) to 25 (`z`), not in string order.

recap: A frequency array uses the value as the index: `freq[x]`.
Set it to 1 to record presence, or use `++` to count.
It must start at zero, and it must be bigger than the largest value.
Looping over the frequency array gives the values in sorted order for free.

check_yourself.q: After counting `2, 4, 3, 4, 5` into `freq`, what are `freq[4]` and `freq[0]`?
In a letter-count array, which letter does index 7 belong to?
When is a frequency array a bad idea?
check_yourself.a: When values can be huge (for example up to 10^9) or negative. The array would be too big, or the index would be invalid.
